name: Yusuf Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alright. I'm Yusuf, I'm 27, and I run my family's egg farm with my dad. We've got 32,000 free-range hens in four sheds, and about 80 hectares of grass and wheat around them. My dad is slowing down, so day to day it's me and three staff. The eggs go to a packing station that supplies the shops.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the first shed at half five. I walk every shed, listening, because a quiet flock or a noisy one tells you something's wrong. Then it's checking the egg belts, the feed and water lines, and opening the pop holes so the hens can go out on the range. Afternoons are fixing things, collecting floor eggs, and sorting the paperwork for the packing station. I love walking out on the range in the evening with the birds coming back in. What wears me out is bird flu season, when we have to shut them in and everyone's on edge.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how do you use AI, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Amira, we're getting married next spring, and for now I still live in the farmhouse with my parents. Amira works on the front desk at a dental surgery. I don't use AI, and I don't really want to. The sheds have computer controls for the fans and lights, but those were put in by my grandad's generation, more or less. We've got about three months' money saved, most of it going on the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I've always thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of noise from people who've never kept a hen. Hens need someone who notices things. A computer can count eggs, it can't tell you a bird is off her food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be pleased. I don't trust it, and I don't like being told I need it. This would just prove that good stockmanship still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep the flock healthy, keep the staff, get married in the spring. Dad and I would carry on with the plan to put up a fifth shed in a few years if the bank agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like an evening when every bird's back in the shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use it for anything at all, like the paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Amira's sister does our books, and she does them well. I'd rather pay a person in the family than a machine in America.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who've never kept a hen. Who do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones on the television telling us how to farm. City people, mostly, and the big companies selling the gadgets. They mean well some of them, but they've never been up at five in a frost.

S0.say: I'd say it was a lot of noise from people who've never kept a hen. A computer can count eggs, but it can't tell you a bird is off her food.
S0.think: Privately I'd be pleased, because I don't trust AI and don't like being told I need it. This would prove good stockmanship still matters.
S0.do: Carries on with the flock and keeps his three staff. Gets married in the spring and keeps the plan to build a fifth hen shed in a few years, if the bank agrees.
S0.feel: Calm and satisfied, like every bird back in the shed at dusk.
S0.quote: A computer can count eggs, it can't tell you a bird is off her food.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf's identity is family stockmanship, and he distrusts both city voices and gadget companies. He'd rather pay a family member than use a tool. The plateau simply confirms his view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. I don't like the sound of that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms should be free to choose, not pushed by rules or by the supermarkets. If a farmer wants robots, fine, if he doesn't, leave him alone. I'd say that at the poultry meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the packing station will start asking for things only the new systems can do, data on every flock, cameras in the sheds. They'll make it a condition of the contract. Then it's not really a choice, is it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off as long as I could. If the packing station made it a condition, I'd get the cheapest system that meets it and have one of the staff learn it. I'd keep spending careful, especially with the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like seeing the packing station's lorry turn up late with a new driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the staff would learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bilal, probably. He's 22 and he's always on his phone anyway. I'd rather he did it than me, and he'd be good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it became a condition of the contract, could you go somewhere else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's one other packer within reach, and they'd want the same. Or we sell at the farm gate, but that's a few hundred eggs a day, not 28,000. So no, not really.

S1.say: I'd say farms should be free to choose, not pushed by rules or supermarkets. If a farmer wants robots, fine, if not, leave him alone.
S1.think: Privately I think the packing station will make data and shed cameras a condition of the contract. Then it isn't really a choice.
S1.do: Holds off as long as possible, then buys the cheapest system that meets the packer's conditions and has a young staff member, Bilal, learn it. Keeps spending careful around the wedding.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a sense of being pushed rather than choosing.
S1.quote: They'll make it a condition of the contract. Then it's not really a choice, is it?
S1.fieldNote: Yusuf frames this as freedom of choice, but privately expects the buyer to force his hand. He'd hand the new tools to a younger worker rather than learn them. He has little room to switch buyers, which he admits plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd be married six months. God help us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities have to look after each other, because you can't wait for the government. Farms like ours should stick together and buy from each other. I'd say it at the mosque and to everyone at the feed merchant's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the big egg companies would put in robot sheds and undercut us within a year. They've got the money and we haven't. My dad built this, and I'd be the one who lost it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything, the honeymoon, the fifth shed, all of it. I'd start selling eggs direct, at the gate and to a few shops in town, so we're not just at the packer's mercy. Dad and I would ask the family whether anyone could help with a loan if we needed one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep. I'd be walking the sheds at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you can't wait for the government. Would you take help if it was offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was for keeping the farm going, yes. If it's just money for doing nothing, no. My dad never took a handout in his life, and I'd feel ashamed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Amira say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say we'd manage, because she's stronger than me about these things. She'd keep her job at the dentist's, if that's still a job. I'd hate living on her money, but I'd have to.

S2.say: I'd say families and communities have to look after each other, because you can't wait for the government. Farms like ours should stick together and buy from each other.
S2.think: Privately I think the big egg companies would put in robot sheds and undercut us within a year. My dad built this, and I'd be the one who lost it.
S2.do: Cuts everything including the honeymoon and the fifth shed. Starts selling eggs direct at the gate and to shops in town, and asks family for a loan if needed, while refusing support that isn't tied to keeping the farm going.
S2.feel: Alarmed, sleepless and ashamed at the thought of losing the family farm.
S2.quote: My dad built this, and I'd be the one who lost it.
S2.fieldNote: Yusuf's fear in the fast picture is about family honour more than money. He'd turn to family, faith community and direct selling, and he draws a firm line between help to keep working and handouts. He'd accept living on his wife's income only with real reluctance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more time, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to build up the family farm's name, so people buy from us because they know us. Real eggs from a real family. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think the name would be enough. The packer would still take most of our eggs, and they'd go with whoever's cheapest. But I'd rather try than give up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start the farm-gate stall properly, with a sign and an honesty box, and get a few local shops and cafés. I'd still hold off on robots until we had to. Amira and I would keep the wedding small and put the rest into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But it's a working anxious, not a lying-awake one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said gate sales were only a few hundred eggs a day. Does five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You're right, I did say that. With five years maybe it's a thousand a day, plus the shops. It's still not 28,000, but it's something nobody can take away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever learn the new systems yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, near the end. I'd rather Bilal did. But if it was that or losing the farm, I'd sit down and learn it, and I wouldn't enjoy it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to build up the family farm's name so people buy from us because they know us. Real eggs from a real family.
S3.think: Privately I don't think the name would be enough, because the packer would still go with whoever's cheapest. But I'd rather try than give up.
S3.do: Sets up a proper farm-gate stall and supplies local shops and cafés in year one. Holds off on robots until forced, keeps the wedding small and puts the rest into savings.
S3.feel: Anxious, but busy rather than sleepless.
S3.quote: It's still not 28,000, but it's something nobody can take away.
S3.fieldNote: Given five years, Yusuf builds a direct-selling side of the business as a shield, while admitting it can't replace the packer contract. When challenged on his earlier numbers he concedes honestly. He'd learn the new systems himself only as a last resort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Then I'd be 37. Dad would be retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for families to prepare without anyone telling them how. Train the young ones, apprenticeships on farms, not just courses on a screen. That's what I'd want to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I get to run the farm properly, and maybe hand on something to my own children one day. If robots come at the end, at least I'd have had my time. That matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and build the farm-gate business slowly. I'd still put up the fifth shed, maybe in year three, if the bank agreed. Around year six, if it was clear the robots were coming, I'd let Bilal set up whatever we needed, so we're not left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Uneasy now and then when I think about the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hand something on to your own children. Does the timing change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. If I knew a robot would do it all, would I want my son to take this on? I don't know. Maybe I'd want him to learn it anyway, the way I learned from my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still build the fifth shed. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But a shed full of hens is worth something, whoever looks after them. If I don't build it, someone bigger will.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for families to prepare without being told how. Train the young ones with apprenticeships on farms, not just courses on a screen.
S4.think: Privately, ten years means I get to run the farm properly and maybe hand something on to my own children. If robots come at the end, at least I'd have had my time.
S4.do: Carries on and grows the farm-gate business slowly. Builds the fifth hen shed around year three if the bank agrees, and around year six lets a younger staff member set up the automation they need.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with some unease about the end point.
S4.quote: If I knew a robot would do it all, would I want my son to take this on?
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Yusuf keep his family story intact for a while: run the farm, marry, maybe pass it on. He'd still invest in a new shed, seeing hens as an asset whoever tends them. The question of handing the farm to a child came up unprompted and clearly weighed on him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My dad built this farm and I'd lose it in two years, right after the wedding. What would help is fair contracts, so the packer can't just switch to whoever has robots, and loans for family farms to keep going, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. I don't know what a robot farm means for people like me, but I know what my community means. Whatever happens, they'll be there, and that's worth more than the money.

headlineQuote: My dad built this, and I'd be the one who lost it.
portrait: Yusuf is a 27-year-old who runs his family's 32,000-hen free-range egg farm with his semi-retired father, and is getting married next spring. He's traditional, values family, faith and hard work, and dislikes both handouts and being told how to farm by city voices or gadget companies. He never uses AI and would hand any new system to a younger worker. His deepest fear is losing what his father built, and his answers swing from proud calm in the plateau to sleepless alarm in the two-year picture, with direct selling as his shield.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd lose the farm his father built within two years, right after his wedding.
whatWouldHelp: Fair contracts so the packer can't simply switch to robot farms, and loans that help family farms keep going rather than handouts.
